name: David Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello David, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a country builder, Fenwick and Sons, and we do mostly farm work: big timber-framed sheds, barn conversions, a few holiday lodges up on the hill. This month it's turning an old stone threshing barn into a house, which means a new oak roof inside old walls that lean every which way. First thing every morning I've got the AI on my tablet sorting the day's cut list and the timber order, and I fly a little drone over roofs to survey them instead of climbing up. I love the oak, the smell and the weight of it. What wears me out is the drive, forty minutes of farm lanes each way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into the tech side, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've always been the one who reads the manual. When drones came out I bought one with my own money and showed Mr Fenwick what it could do on a roof survey. Money is the sore point. I tried to start my own firm at fifty, timber frames, and the downturn finished it in eighteen months, so the savings went with it. My wife Lise works in the school kitchen, the kids are grown, and we've got maybe two weeks in the bank. Fenwick pays fair for round here, which is still less than the towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and that's all, which is what I've been telling the doubters for years anyway. I'd keep showing people the useful bits. On the builders' forum I'm on, I'd probably write something about using it sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means not much changes for me. I keep my edge with the tablet and the drone, and Fenwick keeps me on till I'm done. I'd have liked a bit more excitement, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, using the AI every day for orders and quotes. Maybe I'd do a bit on the side, drawing up barn conversion plans for other small builders with the software, a few hundred pounds a month. And try to build back some of what I lost on the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Drawing plans on the side. Is that something you've done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice, for a mate who builds stables. I used the AI to check the span tables and the software to draw it, and he paid me four hundred each time. If I did it properly, that's a steady trickle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have liked more excitement. Even after losing your savings on your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I don't mean gambling again. The firm taught me that the hard way. I mean I like it when there's something new to get my teeth into.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a decent tool and nothing more, as he's told doubters for years, and write on his builders' forum about using it sensibly.
S0.think: Privately not much changes: he keeps his edge with the tablet and drone and stays with the firm until he's done, though he'd have liked more excitement.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for orders and quotes, and draws barn conversion plans for small builders on the side for a few hundred pounds a month. Tries to rebuild the savings lost on his failed firm.
S0.quote: I don't mean gambling again. The firm taught me that the hard way.
S0.fieldNote: He is the tech enthusiast of his firm, using a drone and AI daily. His thin savings come from a failed attempt to start his own business, which has made him wary of big risks. He already earns a little on the side drawing plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for people who get stuck in early. Some jobs shrink, sure, but there's work for people who can run the new stuff. I'd tell the younger lads to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be all right, maybe better than all right. Fenwick needs someone who can work the new kit, and that's me. The worry is that small firms like Fenwick can't afford the kit and lose work to the big outfits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Mr Fenwick in the first month with a plan: try a robotic cutting machine on one job, rented, not bought. I'd learn it on weekends. I'd grow the plan-drawing on the side, and I'd tell the lads how to use the AI for their own quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Bit of a buzz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Fenwick says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep showing him, like I did with the drone. He said no to that too, then he saw the roof survey done in twenty minutes instead of half a day. He's not daft, he's careful with money, which I should've been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Fenwick's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Fenwick's son, Tom. He's meant to take over and he hates computers. If Tom doesn't move with it, the firm doesn't either, and then none of us have jobs.

S1.say: He'd call it good news for those who get in early, with work for people who can run the new kit, and urge younger workers to start now.
S1.think: Privately he expects to do well as the one who can work the new kit, but worries small firms like his can't afford it and lose work to big outfits.
S1.do: Pitches his boss in the first month on renting a robotic cutting machine for one job and learns it on weekends. Grows his side plan-drawing work and teaches colleagues to use AI for quotes.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a bit of a buzz.
S1.quote: He said no to that too, then he saw the roof survey done in twenty minutes instead of half a day.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an opportunity and knows how to win over a cautious boss. His real worry is the firm's future under the boss's technophobic son. He is careful to suggest renting kit rather than buying, a lesson from his own failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's be practical. Get the kit, get trained, look after people who lose out. I wouldn't be on the barricades, but I'd say the government needs to help small firms get the machines, not just the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's harder than I'd admit. If the robots can do the whole job, my edge is gone in a year or so. Being the one who runs the machine is only a job if someone needs a person there. And I've got nothing in the bank to ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd be on Fenwick's doorstep with a plan to get a robot rig in, and me running it. I'd sell my drone and the spare tools I don't need. I'd try to turn the plan-drawing into something bigger, helping farmers get their sheds designed and built by robots. Lise would take any extra hours at the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, a bit thrilled, a bit sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the two years of warning help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough to get in position, to be the go-to man round here for the robot stuff. It's not enough to rebuild savings. If it went wrong, we'd be properly stuck, and I've been properly stuck once already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers. Why farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know them. I've built sheds for half the farms in the valley. They trust me. They'd rather have someone they know telling them what the robot's doing than a salesman from the city.

S2.say: He'd say it's here so be practical: get the kit, get trained, look after those who lose out, and have the government help small firms afford machines too.
S2.think: Privately it's harder than he'd admit: if robots do the whole job his edge lasts a year or so, and he has nothing saved to ride it out.
S2.do: Pitches his boss in the first month on a robot rig he would run, and sells his drone and spare tools. Tries to grow his side work into helping local farmers get sheds designed and built by robots, while his wife takes extra hours.
S2.feel: Anxious: busy, a bit thrilled and a bit sick.
S2.quote: Being the one who runs the machine is only a job if someone needs a person there.
S2.fieldNote: He moves fast, but he sees clearly that adaptability alone won't protect him under full AGI. The memory of being stuck after his firm failed hangs over his plans. His niche idea rests on trust built with local farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up. Small firms, farmers, everyone can plan. I'd be telling people on the forum to get started now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better for me. I'd be sixty-three, and I'd have time to build up the farm business properly, maybe with a robot rig of my own by year three. I could actually get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, learn everything, run Fenwick's first robot job. Year two, start the farm design business properly, on the side. Year three, maybe go full-time at it, if it's paying. And put money aside every month this time, not like before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "this time". What would you do differently from your first firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not borrow. Start small, on the side, and only jump when the money's coming in. Last time I quit Fenwick's, took a loan for the workshop and then the work dried up. This time Fenwick's is the safety net till it's not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time actually give you, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to prove it works before I bet on it. With two years I'd be jumping in blind. Five, I can watch, try, and jump when it's right.

S3.say: He'd call five years a fair run-up for small firms and farmers to plan, and urge people on his forum to start now.
S3.think: Privately it's better for him: at 63 he'd have time to build his farm business, maybe with his own robot rig by year three, and get ahead.
S3.do: Learns the kit and runs his firm's first robot job in year one, builds a farm design business on the side in year two, and goes full-time in year three only if it pays. Saves monthly and avoids borrowing.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but able to see a path.
S3.quote: This time Fenwick's is the safety net till it's not needed.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him plan carefully, using lessons from his failed business. He'd keep his job as a safety net and avoid debt. He feels he could actually get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who wants to adjust can. I'd be on the forum telling people exactly what to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, and with ten years I could build something steady for my last working years. The farm design business, a robot rig, maybe Tom Fenwick as a partner if he's come round. I'd feel all right about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Fenwick's while I build the side business slowly. Learn every new bit of kit as it arrives, and save properly. By year five or six, decide whether to go out on my own, with money behind me this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite looking forward to it, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money's still thin, so if I got ill, we'd be in trouble. And I'd worry about the young lads in the valley, there won't be the apprenticeships there were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lise say about you going out on your own again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, "not again, David." Then she'd ask what's different, and I'd show her the numbers. If there's money in the bank and work coming in, she'd say go. If not, she'd say no, and she'd be right.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift that lets anyone adjust, and tell people on his forum exactly what to learn.
S4.think: Privately at 68 he could build something steady for his last working years: the farm design business, a robot rig, maybe a partnership with the boss's son.
S4.do: Keeps his job while slowly building the side business, learns each new piece of kit and saves properly. Around year five or six decides whether to go out on his own, only with money behind him.
S4.feel: Calm, even looking forward to it.
S4.quote: She'd say, "not again, David." Then she'd ask what's different, and I'd show her the numbers.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits his temperament: time to try things without betting the house. Thin savings and his wife's caution keep his plans grounded. His remaining worries are illness and fewer apprenticeships for young people locally.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even being quick on the uptake, I've got no money to fall back on, and I've already been stuck once. What would help is help for small firms to get the machines, so it's not just the big outfits, and some kind of cushion for people who lose out while they find their feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about apprenticeships. When I was sixteen, Mr Fenwick's dad took me on. If the robots come, who takes on the sixteen-year-olds? Somebody needs to think about that.

headlineQuote: I've built sheds for half the farms in the valley. They trust me.
portrait: David Jensen is a 58-year-old lead carpenter for a country builder doing barn conversions and farm sheds, who surveys roofs with his own drone and uses AI every day. He lost his savings when his own firm failed at 50, and that has taught him to rent rather than buy and to keep his job as a safety net. He welcomes steady change, and even under AGI in two years he moves fast, though he admits being the machine operator only works if someone still needs a person. With five or ten years he plans to build a farm design business slowly and feels quite hopeful.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even moving quickly he has no money to fall back on and has been stuck once before.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small firms to get the machines, not just big outfits, and a cushion for people who lose out while they find their feet.
